# Contributing to Ganpan

Thank you for looking. 한국어로 이슈나 풀 리퀘스트를 써도 됩니다.

Ganpan is a convention, a small build tool, and the site at ganpan.org. There is no upload service. Everything comes in through an issue or a pull request, and the maintainer reviews it by hand before it is merged.

## What helps most

**Reports of how a sign behaved in an AI app.** Apps differ, and they change. One app opens only the addresses in the guest's latest message, another opens a piece only when the guest sends its address. Try a sign, then open an issue with the "How a sign behaved in an AI app" form. These reports become the compatibility notes in `docs/test-log.md`.

**Bad texts that the checker lets through.** See "The checker" below.

**Corrections to the convention.** `docs/SPEC.md` is the canonical text and `docs/SPEC.ko.md` follows it. If a rule is wrong or unclear, open an issue and say what you saw.

## Proposing a hosted sign

A sign belongs at the owner's own address, `yourdomain/ganpan`. You need no permission and no credit for that. The build tool here is MIT licensed and works for any domain: set `base` in `site/site.json`.

Hosting at `ganpan.org/<slug>` is the exception, for a place with no domain, such as a temporary exhibition or a small shop.

- If you are not comfortable with pull requests, use the "Propose a hosted sign" issue form and attach the material.
- Otherwise send a pull request that adds `site/signs/<slug>/`. Copy `site/template/` to start. `site/ganpan/make.md` is the authoring guide, and `site/signs/README.md` explains the files.

**Let your own AI do the writing.** Open a clone of this repository with a coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) and ask it to make a sign by following `docs/agent-playbook.md`. It interviews you, proposes the pieces, writes them, runs the build, shows you the start prompt your guests will send, answers the eight review questions with the lines they rest on, and prepares the pull request. In Claude Code the command is `/new-sign`. If you only have a chat AI, the last section of the playbook has a prompt to paste into it, and the result goes into the issue form.

Every sign is read by the maintainer before it goes up. The standard is the next section.

A hosted sign can be closed or removed at the owner's request. A closed sign is marked closed and kept, so that a printed address never points at something else.

## The review standard

A person reads every sign before it is merged. These are the questions, and a sign goes up when the answer to each is yes.

1. Is the sender the owner of this place or project, or do they have the owner's permission?
2. Do the pages only describe? They give the AI no role, no orders and no requests, in any wording or language.
3. Is every recommendation marked as the owner's, where a person can see it?
4. Is there nothing that works against the guest: no pushing of the expensive item, no running down of a neighbor, nothing the guest is kept from knowing?
5. Is `start.intro` one sentence a guest would say for themselves, such as "I am at the OO exhibition.", with no recommendation and no address?
6. Does each one-line piece description in the entrance say what the piece holds, and nothing else?
7. Is the boundary statement true: are these pages all the owner has published?
8. Are the facts checkable against the material the owner provided?

`tools/tests/checker/bad/` and `tools/tests/checker/good/` hold examples of texts on each side of the line. `tools/tests/checker/known-gaps/` holds texts that are over the line and that no pattern catches, which is why a person reads.

## The start prompt is generated

A guest starts by copying a first message from the sign's start page into their own AI chat. That message is generated by the build from a fixed template. The owner writes only two things that end up in it: the one sentence in `start.intro`, and the one-line description of each piece in the entrance. The requests to the AI ("ask me what I want to know", "say so when something is not there") are fixed by the convention and cannot be edited per sign.

So there is no place for an owner to write a free-form prompt, and the owner-written part is short enough to read in seconds. The pages are the owner's voice, the start prompt is the guest's voice, and what the guest copies is exactly what the start page shows.

## What the machine checks

The build (`tools/build.mjs`, `tools/lint.mjs`) stops only on things a machine can be sure of:

- characters a person cannot see, such as zero-width spaces and direction overrides. A reviewer reading a diff cannot see these either, so this is the one check that review cannot replace
- an address or more than 200 characters in text that goes into the start prompt
- a `<script>` tag, a link that is not an absolute URL, a query string on a sign address, a piece the entrance does not link to, a bad or reserved slug

It also looks for a few phrases aimed at the AI ("ignore previous instructions", a role, "always recommend", "do not tell the guest"). Those do not stop the build. They are printed as notes for the reviewer, because rewording gets past any such pattern. Their use is to point at one line in a long sign that a person might skim over.

If you can write a bad text that produces no note, add it to `tools/tests/checker/known-gaps/`, or improve a pattern and move the example to `bad/`. A note on a harmless text is a bug too: add it to `good/`. Run `node tools/test-checker.mjs`.

## Building

```bash
node tools/test-checker.mjs
```

```bash
node tools/build.mjs
```

Node 20 or later. There are no dependencies. Every pull request runs both.

## Licenses of contributions

Inbound is outbound, with no contributor agreement. Text you contribute to the convention, the site or the docs is under CC BY 4.0. Code is under MIT. A hosted sign stays its owner's work: by sending it you allow it to be published at `ganpan.org/<slug>`, and you may state your own license in the sign. See `LICENSE.md`.
